question: Starting with which fiscal year does NVIDIA discuss NVIDIA's H20 chips in its 10-K risk factors (Item 1A) or MD&A (Item 7)?
answer:
**NVIDIA's fiscal year 2026** (10-K dated January 25, 2026) — that is the first year within the five years of filings covered (FY2022–FY2026) in which H20 appears in Item 1A or Item 7.

What it says in FY2026:
- Item 1A / Item 7: in April 2025 the U.S. government informed NVIDIA that a license is required for exports of its H20 integrated circuits (and any circuits meeting H20's memory/interconnect bandwidth) to China, Hong Kong, Macau and D:5 countries; as a result NVIDIA incurred a **$4.5 billion charge in Q1 FY2026** for excess inventory and purchase obligations tied to H20 [3][4][15].
- Item 1A/1: in August 2025 the USG granted licenses allowing shipment of certain H20 products to certain China-based customers, under which NVIDIA generated **approximately $60 million** in H20 revenue [1][5][9].
- Item 1A also notes China's government publicly questioned whether H20 products had built-in vulnerabilities, discouraging purchases [13].

No mention of H20 in FY2024 or FY2025 Items 1A/7 — those filings discuss only the earlier A100/A800/H100/H800/L40S and Blackwell restrictions [17][18][19][22][23]. One FY2025 passage that surfaces on an "H20" keyword search in fact lists "H200" (not H20), so it is not an H20 disclosure [6].

question: In which fiscal year's 10-K did NVIDIA first mention the EU AI Act in its 10-K risk factors (Item 1A) or MD&A (Item 7)?
answer:
**NVIDIA's fiscal 2024 10-K** (fiscal year ended January 28, 2024) — Item 1A, Risk Factors.

The claim history for NVDA's legal/regulatory disclosures (covering FY2022–FY2026) shows no EU AI Act mention in FY2022 or FY2023, then a **new** FY2024 risk-factor statement: "Furthermore, the EU AI Act could impose onerous obligations that may disproportionately impact and disadvantage us and require us to change our business practices" [1]. The same language appears in the FY2024 filing text [9].

It was then expanded in FY2025, which added that the Act "became effective on August 1, 2024 and will be fully applicable after a two-year transitional period" [2][8], and carried forward substantially unchanged in FY2026 [4][5][6].

question: In which fiscal year's 10-K did AMD first mention ZT Systems in its 10-K risk factors (Item 1A) or MD&A (Item 7)?
answer:
AMD first mentioned **ZT Systems in its FY2024 10-K** (fiscal year ended December 28, 2024). The disclosure was new that year, with no ZT Systems mentions in the FY2021–FY2023 10-Ks [1].

In that FY2024 filing, AMD discussed the pending acquisition in both:
- **Item 1A (Risk Factors)** — closing conditions, regulatory approvals, and a potential $300 million termination fee [12].
- **MD&A/business discussion** — the August 2024 agreement to acquire ZT Systems, expected to close in the first half of 2025 [1][4].

question: When did the EU AI Act first show up in the risk factors (Item 1A) or MD&A (Item 7) of AMD's annual reports?
answer:
**AMD's EU AI Act mention first appeared in the FY2023 10-K** (fiscal year ended Dec. 30, 2023), in **Item 1A (Risk Factors)** — not in MD&A.

- **FY2023** — new that year: *"For example, in the EU, an AI act is being considered."* [1][4]
- **FY2024** — wording changed to reflect adoption: *"the EU AI Act was adopted in 2024 and its implementation will be phased in over the next few years."* [2][6]
- **FY2025** — carried forward essentially unchanged [3][7]

No mention appears in AMD's FY2021 or FY2022 filings, the earliest years covered by the claims data (FY2021–FY2025) [1]. All three mentions are in Item 1A; no MD&A occurrence was found.

question: When did Section 232 investigations first show up in the risk factors (Item 1A) or MD&A (Item 7) of Analog Devices's annual reports?
answer: Within the available data (ADI’s FY2021–FY2025 annual reports), **Section 232 investigations first appear in FY2025**, in **Item 1A, Risk Factors**. The FY2025 filing states that “throughout 2025 the U.S. government has initiated numerous investigations into products and industries under Section 232,” citing the April 2025 Commerce Department investigation into imported semiconductors and semiconductor manufacturing equipment [1][2]. Claim history marks this as **new in FY2025**; no Section 232 mention appears in FY2021–FY2024 [1].

question: Starting with which fiscal year does Lam Research discuss rare earth elements in its 10-K risk factors (Item 1A) or MD&A (Item 7)?
answer:
**Fiscal year 2025** (10-K for the year ended June 29, 2025) — and it appears in **Item 1A (Risk Factors)**, not MD&A.

**How it evolved:**

| FY | Where | What it says |
|---|---|---|
| 2022–2024 | — | No discussion of rare earth elements found in the 10-K text (the FY2024 supply-risk bullets, for example, mention "rising inflation or interest rates" and "import or export approvals" but no rare earths) [23] |
| **2025** | Item 1A | First mention, framed around downstream customers: "certain materials are primarily available in a limited number of countries, including rare earth elements, minerals, and metals," which could impair customers' ability to source inputs and thus demand for Lam's products [2] |
| 2026 | Item 1A (expanded) | Upgraded to a direct supply risk: "China is the primary source of supply of certain rare earth elements critical to the manufacture of certain of our products," plus Chinese export controls and license requirements on rare earth elements and on products containing Chinese-origin rare earths (partly suspended until November 2026 unless extended) [1][2→1], new this year per claim history [21]; also new language about "Chinese export controls on rare earth elements" as a source of export-approval delay risk [4] |

The claim-tracking data confirms the substance was new in FY2026: the supplier-dependence claim "China is the primary source of supply of certain rare earth elements…" is flagged **new this year** [21], as is the export-controls claim on Chinese rare earth license requirements [22]. The FY2025 filing's coverage was the earlier, more generic customer-impact framing [3→2].

No rare earth discussion was found in Item 7 (MD&A) for either FY2025 or FY2026 [28][29][30][31][32].

question: Starting with which fiscal year does Marvell discuss Silicon Valley Bank in its 10-K risk factors (Item 1A) or MD&A (Item 7)?
answer:
Marvell first discusses Silicon Valley Bank in its **fiscal 2024 10-K** (fiscal year ended February 3, 2024), within **Item 1A, Risk Factors** [2][6].

The disclosure states that SVB, where Marvell held an immaterial amount of cash deposits, was placed into FDIC receivership on March 10, 2023, and that access to its accounts was fully restored by March 13, 2023 [2][6]. question: NVIDIA used to discuss the terminated Arm acquisition in its 10-K risk factors (Item 1A) or MD&A (Item 7). Which fiscal year's filing was the last to mention it?
answer:
The last filing to mention the terminated Arm acquisition in either Item 1A or Item 7 was NVIDIA’s **FY2024 10-K** (fiscal year ended January 28, 2024).

Its MD&A still referred to fiscal 2023’s **“$1.4 billion acquisition termination charge related to the proposed Arm transaction”** [17] and included an “Acquisition Termination Cost” discussion stating the charge related to the Arm transaction [18]. So: **FY2024 was the last 10-K to mention it; more specifically, FY2023 was the last 10-K to mention it in Item 1A, while FY2024 was the last to mention it in Item 7.**

question: What was the last fiscal year in which Applied Materials mentioned COVID-19 in its 10-K risk factors (Item 1A) or MD&A (Item 7)?
answer:
**Applied Materials' last fiscal year mentioning COVID-19 in Item 1A or Item 7 was FY2022** (fiscal year ended October 30, 2022).

- In the FY2022 10-K, Item 1A included a dedicated risk factor: "The continued effects of the COVID-19 pandemic and global measures taken in response have adversely impacted, and may continue to adversely impact, Applied's operations and financial results," describing supply chain, logistics, workforce and remote-work cybersecurity impacts [1].
- FY2022 MD&A (Item 7) also discussed it, including a section "Applied's Pandemic Response" noting measures taken "as the COVID-19 pandemic emerged in 2020" and that "the situation remains fluid and uncertain" [2][3].
- By **FY2023** (10-K filed for fiscal year ended October 29, 2023), the dedicated COVID-19 risk factor and pandemic discussion were gone; the filing instead refers only generically to "regional or global health epidemics" among other disruption events [25], with no COVID-19-specific language in Item 1A [21][22][23][24] or Item 7 [12][14][15].
- FY2024 and FY2025 likewise contain no COVID-19 references in those sections — only generalized language such as "regional or global health epidemics" [8] and, in FY2025, cybersecurity/AI and quantum-computing risk topics [16][18][20].

Note: the search index covers each company's last five fiscal years, so "last" here is bounded by that coverage (FY2021–FY2025 for AMAT).

So, across either section, **COVID-19 last appeared in Qualcomm’s FY2023 10-K**, within Item 1A.

question: Is the EU Digital Markets Act still mentioned in the risk factors (Item 1A) or MD&A (Item 7) in Microsoft's latest 10-K? If not, when did it last appear?

question: How did Applied Materials's share of net sales (net revenue) to customers outside the United States change from fiscal 2021 to fiscal 2025? Give each year's figure.
answer:
**Applied Materials — net revenue to customers outside the United States (fiscal years end late October)**

| Fiscal year | Net revenue outside U.S. | Total net revenue | Share outside U.S. |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2021 | $21,025M | $23,063M | 91.2% |
| 2022 | $22,681M (derived) | $25,785M | 88.0% (derived) |
| 2023 | $22,511M | $26,517M | 84.9% |
| 2024 | $23,358M | $27,176M | 85.9% |
| 2025 | $25,305M | $28,368M | 89.2% |

Sources and notes:
- FY2021 figures as reported [6]; share calculated as 21,025 / 23,063 = 91.2% [6].
- FY2022: the filing reports U.S. net sales of $3,104M against a $25,785M total [12]; the non-U.S. amount and share are therefore **derived** (25,785 − 3,104 = 22,681; 22,681 / 25,785 = 88.0%), since no "Total outside United States" line was returned for that year [12].
- FY2023: 22,511 / 26,517 = 84.9% [3]; FY2024: 23,358 / 27,176 = 85.9% [3]; FY2025: 25,305 / 28,368 = 89.2% [3].
- FY2025 corroboration: Applied states "approximately 89% of our net revenue was to customers in regions outside the United States" [1].

**Change:** The non-U.S. share fell from 91.2% in fiscal 2021 to 89.2% in fiscal 2025, a decline of 2.0 percentage points [6][3], with the low point in fiscal 2023 (84.9%) as U.S. revenue rose [3][18]. Absolute non-U.S. revenue still grew from $21,025M to $25,305M [6][3].

**What I could not find:** I did not locate a filing passage explicitly stating a "percent of net sales outside the United States" figure for FY2021–FY2024; those percentages are computed from the reported regional dollar amounts.

question: How did Microsoft's effective tax rate change from fiscal 2022 to fiscal 2026? Give each year's figure.
answer:
**Microsoft's effective tax rate, fiscal 2022 → fiscal 2026** (fiscal years ended June 30):

| Fiscal year | Effective tax rate |
|---|---|
| 2022 | 13% [5] |
| 2023 | 19% [2] |
| 2024 | 18% [3] |
| 2025 | 18% [1] |
| 2026 | 19% [4] |

**Change:** up 6.0 percentage points, from 13% to 19% [5][4].

Drivers:
- FY2022's unusually low 13% reflected a **$3.3 billion net income tax benefit** in Q1 FY2022 from transferring certain intangible properties from a Puerto Rico subsidiary to the U.S. [5][2].
- The FY2023 jump to 19% was due to that prior-year benefit plus a decrease in tax benefits related to stock-based compensation [2].
- FY2024 dipped to 18% on tax benefits from IRS/Treasury Notices 2023-55 and 2023-80, which delayed the effective date of final foreign tax credit regulations [3].
- FY2026's rise from 18% to 19% was primarily due to changes in the mix of earnings and tax expenses between the U.S. and foreign countries [4].

Across all years the rate stayed below the U.S. federal statutory rate, mainly because of earnings taxed at lower rates in foreign jurisdictions through Microsoft's regional operations center in Ireland [1][4].

question: How did Broadcom's risk-factor statement about its largest end customers change between its fiscal 2023 and fiscal 2024 10-Ks?
answer:
**Short answer:** Broadcom removed its explicit naming of Apple and stopped quantifying Apple's share of revenue; the only remaining customer-concentration figure is a bigger top-five aggregate.

**FY2023 10-K (fiscal year ended Oct. 29, 2023)** — the risk factor *named* Apple and gave both numbers [18]:

> "For fiscal year 2023, sales to distributors accounted for 57% of our net revenue. We believe aggregate sales, through all channels, to Apple and our top five end customers, accounted for approximately 20% and 35% of our net revenue for fiscal year 2023, respectively." [18]

It also named the distributor: "Direct sales to WT Microelectronics Co., Ltd., a distributor, accounted for 21% and 20% of our net revenue for fiscal years 2023 and 2022" [7].

**FY2024 10-K (fiscal year ended Nov. 3, 2024)** — Apple is gone from the disclosure entirely [23]:

> "For fiscal year 2024, sales to distributors accounted for 48% of our net revenue. We believe aggregate sales, through all channels, to our top five end customers accounted for approximately 40% of our net revenue for fiscal year 2024." [23]

The distributor is no longer named either — it is now "one customer, which is a distributor," at 28% of net revenue (vs. 21% in FY2023) [16].

**What changed, point by point:**
- **Apple de-identified:** the FY2023 sentence quantifying Apple at ~20% [9] *does not appear* in the FY2024 filing — the only dropped customer-concentration claim between the two years [9]/[10]. Apple and the prior-year ~20% figure disappear; investors can no longer see the Apple-specific share.
- **Top-five concentration rose:** ~35% of net revenue in FY2023 → ~40% in FY2024, a 5-percentage-point increase [17].
- **Channel mix shifted:** distributor sales fell from 57% to 48% of net revenue [1]/[15] vs. [13]/[15], while direct sales to the single distributor customer rose to 28% (from 21%) [16].
- **Wording softened slightly:** "adverse developments experienced by our significant customers" (FY2023) became "adverse developments experienced by these customers" (FY2024) [18] vs. [23].
- **Channel-partner risk escalated:** "We expect our dependence on channel partners will increase following the VMware Merger" [19] became "Our dependence on channel partners has increased following the VMware Merger" [24], with added language on go-to-market programs and "certain sole distribution relationships by region" [24].

So the net effect is *less* transparency on the identity of the largest end customer (Apple) but a *higher* disclosed top-five concentration, plus a now-confirmed increase in distributor dependence post-VMware.

question: How did Marvell's wording about its ten largest customers change between the fiscal 2024 and fiscal 2025 10-Ks, and what share did they represent?
answer:
**Wording change (FY2024 → FY2025)**

- **FY2024 10-K:** "In addition, net revenue from our ten (10) largest customers, including this distributor, represented **72%** of our net revenue for the fiscal year ended February 3, 2024." [1]
- **FY2025 10-K:** "In addition, net revenue from our ten (10) largest customers, **inclusive of our distributor and direct customers**, represented **81%** of our **total** net revenue for the fiscal year ended February 1, 2025." [3]

Two shifts in language: the earlier version framed the 10 largest purely around "this distributor," while the later version explicitly says the group includes both the distributor **and direct customers**; and "net revenue" became "total net revenue." [1][3]

**Related context on concentration**

- FY2024: "during fiscal 2024, we had one distributor whose revenue as a percentage of our net revenue was 10% or greater of total net revenues." [4]
- FY2025: "during fiscal 2025, there were two customers (one distributor and one direct customer) whose revenues represented 10% or more of total net revenue." [6]

So over that year, top-ten concentration rose from 72% to 81% of net revenue and the number of ≥10% customers went from one to two. Note the FY2024 figure is restated in the FY2025 filing only as a wording comparison — the 72% is as originally reported for fiscal 2024.

question: What fiscal 2026 charge did NVIDIA take because of the new H20 export license requirement, and what was its total fiscal 2026 revenue and growth?
answer:
**H20 export license charge:** In April 2025, the U.S. government informed NVIDIA that a license is required for exports of its H20 integrated circuits to China (including Hong Kong and Macau) and D:5 countries. As a result, NVIDIA incurred a **$4.5 billion charge in the first quarter of fiscal 2026** associated with H20 for excess inventory and purchase obligations, as demand for H20 products diminished [1][3][5]. (Later, in August 2025, the USG granted licenses allowing shipments of certain H20 products to certain China-based customers, under which NVIDIA generated approximately $60 million in H20 revenue [2][5].)

**Fiscal 2026 revenue and growth:**
- FY2026 revenue (fiscal year ended January 25, 2026): **$215.9 billion** [6]
- FY2025 revenue: $130.5 billion [7]
- Growth: **65.5%** [6][7]

question: What were Qualcomm's fiscal 2025 revenues and net income, and what does the filing say about future product revenue from Huawei?
answer:
**Qualcomm, fiscal year 2025 (ended September 28, 2025):**

| Metric | FY2025 |
|---|---|
| Revenue | $44.28 billion [1] |
| Net income | $5.54 billion [2] |

**Future product revenue from Huawei**

Qualcomm said it expects no further product revenue from Huawei. Per the FY2025 10-K risk factors: in May 2024 the U.S. Department of Commerce revoked the export license under which Qualcomm had been selling 4G and certain other integrated circuit products to Huawei, and "accordingly, we do not expect to receive any further product revenues from Huawei." The filing adds that to the extent Huawei's devices take share from OEMs that use Qualcomm products — in China or elsewhere — results of operations and cash flows could be further impacted [3].

On the licensing side, MD&A notes that beginning in the second quarter of fiscal 2025, QTL revenues no longer included royalties from Huawei, whose license agreement has expired [4].

**Context:** FY2025 QTL licensing revenues were $5,582 million versus $5,572 million in FY2024, essentially flat [4].

question: In fiscal 2025, what share of Broadcom's net revenue came from China, and how much came from its largest direct customer?
answer:
**China (incl. Hong Kong):** Broadcom's fiscal 2025 (ended Nov 2, 2025) net revenue from China was **$11,155 million** out of **$63,887 million** total net revenue [1][22] — about **17.5%** of net revenue (calculated: 11,155 ÷ 63,887) [1][22]. The company itself states that "in fiscal years 2025 and 2024, 17% and 20%, respectively, of our net revenue came from shipments or deliveries to China (including Hong Kong)" [4][20]. Broadcom cautions that these figures reflect shipment/delivery location, not end-customer location, and that a substantially smaller share of revenue is ultimately dependent on end customers in China [3][4].

**Largest direct customer:** Direct sales to one customer — a distributor in the semiconductor solutions segment — accounted for **32% of net revenue** in fiscal 2025 (up from 28% in 2024 and 21% in 2023) [3][5][13]. On a derived basis (not disclosed as a dollar figure), 32% of $63,887 million is roughly **$20.4 billion** [22]. For context, the top five end customers, through all channels, were about 40% of net revenue, and distributors overall were 48% [5][7][8].

Note: the filing does not name the largest customer nor give its revenue in dollars — only the 32% percentage; the ~$20.4 billion is my calculation from total revenue.

question: How many H20 units did NVIDIA ship to China in fiscal 2026?
answer:
**NVIDIA's filings do not disclose an H20 unit shipment count for fiscal 2026.** No tool result provides unit volumes for H20 or any other product line.

What the fiscal 2026 10-K does disclose about H20 and China:

- In April 2025, the U.S. government informed NVIDIA that a license is required to export H20 integrated circuits (and circuits achieving comparable memory/interconnect bandwidth) to China, including Hong Kong and Macau, and D:5 countries. As a result, NVIDIA recorded a **$4.5 billion charge in Q1 FY2026** related to H20 excess inventory and purchase obligations "as the demand for H20 products diminished" [3][4][5].
- In August 2025, the USG granted licenses allowing shipment of certain H20 products to certain China-based customers, and NVIDIA "generated approximately **$60 million** in H20 revenue under those licenses" [1][2][5]. USG officials expressed an expectation of receiving 15% or more of that revenue, though no codifying regulation was published [1][2].
- Separately, a February 2026 license permits "small amounts" of H200 products to specific China-based customers, subject to U.S. inspection and a 25% tariff on import into the U.S.; no revenue had been generated under that program [1][2][6].

So the only quantified H20 China figure in the filing is the ~$60 million of licensed revenue [1] — not a unit count. If you need unit volumes, that would have to come from outside the 10-K (e.g., management commentary), which isn't in the indexed filings.
